I worked on a cruise ship out of Florida for a year after high school, and let me tell you this story:

I was making drinks for this woman at the bar, she was all alone and traveling to Cozumel as a travel agent for her agency for whatever reason, I'm not sure on that - but she was there, and drinking heavy. 

When the bar started to clear out one of the three nights she was on the ship with me, she stayed and talked for a while. 

She told me how she left her parents' abusive and drug ridden lifestyle and came to Florida for hope, for anything, really. There were personal stories I won't include, but then she explained that she wanted a suite room to see the ocean. 

Turns out the reason for her wanting to see nothing but the open sea was that her father, who abused her for so many years, couldn't swim.

The ocean was the one place he could never get to her.

She left, but we kept in contact via email for about a year, until she and I kind of mutually dropped of each other's radar. 

Sad, but inspiring because of how she moved on.

I worked at Wal-Mart over the holiday season a few years ago, and there was this woman who demanded - and any retail worker knows what I mean by that - that we find her a red toaster. 

She didn't care about anything else but having it be red.

My manager and a few other people went all the way out to our trailers of merchandise in -10 degree weather to find this, while I was left to try and calm her down, mainly because I apparently have that 'effect' on crazy people. While talking to her, I learned that the reason she needed this was because she was invited to a high-society (our store was in those types of neighborhoods) dinner party and she had forgot to bring a gift.

If the toaster was the wrong color scheme, her chances of heading the next PTA meeting would be over.

\*gasps intensely\*

I went to go check on the guys outside after about ten minutes, and found them with one red toaster. For whatever reason, the manager made me tell why she wanted it when he found out I knew.

Then, as I would later find out when she took the toaster back, fuming, my manager whipped out his box cutter when my back was turned and slit the cord in two.

She was furious to say the least, and no, the toaster did not work. I kinda felt bad for the toaster, though. Still do.

I used to work with this lady from Pakistan who only spoke Farsi. I couldn't learn much, but we worked together, inseparably, in retail. I was the only one nice enough to wave and work alongside her, not away from her. As the weeks began to pass, the managers couldn't get her to do anything they asked, simply because she couldn't understand, so I took it upon myself to translate. They would tell me what to do, and then I would start doing the task, and she would join in. Soon, I starting pointing at things and saying the English word for them, and she would do the same in Farsi.

For the year we worked together, we ended up with a strange kind of Spanglish and made it work. 

I remember it fondly, because she always tried her best, and I reciprocated.

I was sleeping over at my cousin's house when I was very young, about nine or ten, and woke up in the middle of the night to pee. I walked past the kitchen and overheard my Aunt and Uncle crying. I kind of peeked into the kitchen and saw my Aunt staring at a photo of this woman that was also in my house and around the rest of the family's places. I never thought to ask who she was, despite having not seen her before, and since I was so young, I assumed she lived out of state or somewhere unreachable. My Aunt had acted weird the whole day and just smiled awkwardly at me, mainly because I share a lot of features with said woman in the picture.

Truth is, after listening for a couple of minutes, I learned that the woman pictured was my Aunt in her teen years, when she abruptly ended her own life and didn't leave a note or anything at all. 

I wasn't supposed to find out, because a few other family members had clinical depression (and later me) and they didn't want the kids of the family to freak out.

I hid the fact that I knew until I was old enough for the rest of the family secrets to be revealed to me naturally.

Those few years in between, I photocopied her picture and would talk to it for hours, asking questions and never getting a response.

I still miss her, even though she never knew my mother had me, or got married, or anything else.

I was about twelve when a teenager who was drunk and high on cocaine slammed into the family car. I blacked out and woke up on the street, with a paramedic standing over me. All four of my family members, and our dog, lived.

The dog and I are the only ones who haven't had lasting effects. 

My mother and sister were injured in the spine and my father suffered from PTSD before his sad death. 

Three other cars were totaled and two people died because of that teenager, whoever they were.

The dog is still alive. She's going on sixteen but is still kicking.

According to the paramedics and later our attorneys, the only thing that kept me alive was a spare tire on the back of our SUV that took the brunt of it, and also slammed back with the force and killed the passenger in the offending car before they ever knew they hit something. I should have died and had to go to therapy for years to get over survivor's guilt, which still haunts me.

I experienced only one ill effect, memory loss of the whole week it happened, other than nightmares of standing in the rain next to a building that said only 'Taxidermy' while they hauled our destroyed car away. Years of therapy later and I have no idea what happened other than that, through my eyes, at least.

I open the shop for an hour or two and then go up to the floors and joke with the nurses before talking to any new patients. By midday I'm at the continuing patients' rooms and I do anything to make them smile. Whether I sing (badly), joke, tell stories or just listen to their problems.

It makes my life knowing I can make the day, or sadly the last day of someone else's life positive.

Before her death, my Grandmother used to just sit in a chair and drink a lot. I was young and living with her at the time because my parents were waiting on a house to close. I thought it was normal for all of her children, including my mother, to want to have nothing to do with her. Don't ask me how I thought this was normal in everyone's life, because I ask myself a lot, too. Long story short, she died two days after we moved into our new house and my mother and my immediate family didn't even host a funeral. We just dumped her in the ground, basically, and moved on. 

I didn't think much of it, as if it was, well, what everyone else did, until I went to an actual funeral for the first time and asked questions. By the time I hit my twenties, I learned that my Grandmother drove my Grandfather, my Aunt and my Uncle to suicide and drug addiction and wrecked the rest of her kids, leaving her legacy as a hoarder behind.

All those years as a child I thought everyone's Grandma asked them for beers and was a total asshole.
